<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                <jats:p><jats:italic>Klebsiella</jats:italic> spp. are important pathogens associated with bacteremia among admitted children and is among the leading cause of death in children < 5 years in postmortem studies, supporting a larger role than previously considered in childhood mortality. Herein, we compared the antimicrobial susceptibility, mechanisms of resistance, and the virulence profile of <jats:italic>Klebsiella</jats:italic> spp. from admitted and postmortem children.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                <jats:p>Antimicrobial susceptibility and virulence factors of <jats:italic>Klebsiella</jats:italic> spp. recovered from blood samples collected upon admission to the hospital (<jats:italic>n =</jats:italic> 88) and postmortem blood (<jats:italic>n =</jats:italic> 23) from children < 5 years were assessed by disk diffusion and multiplex PCR.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                <jats:p><jats:italic>Klebsiella</jats:italic> isolates from postmortem blood were likely to be ceftriaxone resistant (69.6%, 16/23 vs. 48.9%, 43/88, <jats:italic>p</jats:italic> = 0.045) or extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) producers (60.9%, 14/23 vs. 25%, 22/88, <jats:italic>p =</jats:italic> 0.001) compared to those from admitted children. bla<jats:sub>CTX-M-15</jats:sub> was the most frequent ESBL gene: 65.3%, 9/14 in postmortem isolates and 22.7% (5/22) from admitted children. We found higher frequency of genes associated with hypermucoviscosity phenotype and invasin in postmortem isolates than those from admitted children: rmpA (30.4%; 7/23 vs. 9.1%, 8/88, <jats:italic>p =</jats:italic> 0.011), <jats:italic>wzi-K1</jats:italic> (34.7%; 8/23 vs. 8%; 7/88, <jats:italic>p =</jats:italic> 0.002) and traT (60.8%; 14/23 vs. 10.2%; 9/88, <jats:italic>p</jats:italic> < 0.0001), respectively. Additionally, serine protease auto-transporters of Enterobacteriaceae were detected from 1.8% (<jats:italic>pic</jats:italic>) to 12.6% (<jats:italic>pet)</jats:italic> among all isolates. <jats:italic>Klebsiella</jats:italic> case fatality rate was 30.7% (23/75).</jats:p>
              </jats:sec><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                <jats:p>Multidrug resistant <jats:italic>Klebsiella</jats:italic> spp. harboring genes associated with hypermucoviscosity phenotype has emerged in Mozambique causing invasive fatal disease in children; highlighting the urgent need for prompt diagnosis, appropriate treatment and effective preventive measures for infection control.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec>
title: Klebsiella spp. cause severe and fatal disease in Mozambican children: antimicrobial resistance profile and molecular characterization
